# Part 1: Data Loading & Validation

## Function 1: Load and Validate Student Data

**Task:** Load a CSV file and validate it has the expected structure.

**Requirements:**

- Return NULL if file doesn't exist (don't throw error)
- Return NULL if file is empty
- Return NULL if required columns are missing: "student_id", "name", "math_score"
- Return the data frame only if all validations pass
- Convert enrollment_date to Date type if present

```{r load_student_data}
# YOUR CODE HERE
load_student_data <- function(student_scores.csv) {
  # TODO: Implement with proper validation
  
  # This is to make sure the input is valid. The function expects a single character value (the file path). If it's NULL and not a character, or has length other than 1, I am returning NULL as a safe failure.
  if(is.null(student_scores.csv) || !is.character(student_scores.csv) || length(student_scores.csv)!=1){
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # Checking whether the file/dataset actually exists. Not throwing any error.
  if (!file.exists(student_scores.csv)) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # This is to read the CSV file. I am wrapping it in tryCatch to prevent the whole script from crashing in the case of failure.
  # Also, (stringsAsFactors = FALSE) is to force the text to stay as characters.
  df <- tryCatch(
    read.csv("student_scores.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
    error = function(e){
      return(NULL)
    }
  )
  
  # In case the read.csv() failed, I am returning NULL.
  if(is.null(df)){
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # In case the file/dataset is empty, I am returning NULL. Basically when there are no rows or columns, it implies the dataset is empty.
  if(nrow(df)==0 || ncol(df)==0){
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # Defining the columns that are mandatory/required for the data to be valid.
  required_cols <- c("student_id", "name", "math_score")
  
  # Checking if all the required columns are present in the dataset, and returning NULL otherwise.
  if(!all(required_cols %in% names(df))){
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # If the enrollment_date column exists, I am converting it to type Date.
  if("enrollment_date" %in% names(df)){
    df$enrollment_date <- as.Date(df$enrollment_date)
  }
  
  # If all the checks are passed successfully, I am returning the validated data frame.
  return(df)
}
```

## Function 2: Filter Students with Incomplete Data

**Task:** Return students who have missing values (NA) in ANY of the score columns.

**Requirements:**

- Check math_score, english_score, science_score columns
- Return data frame with ALL original columns
- Include a new column "missing_count" showing how many scores are missing (1, 2, or 3)
- Sort by missing_count (descending), then by student_id (ascending)
- If no students have missing data, return empty data frame with correct column structure

```{r filter_incomplete_students}
# YOUR CODE HERE
filter_incomplete_students <- function(data) {
  # TODO: Find students with ANY missing scores
  
  # First check is to see if the input is valid. As the function is expecting a data frame, if it is NULL or not a data frame, I am returning an empty data frame.
  if (is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)) {
    return(data.frame(missing_count = integer(0)))
  }
  
  # Specified score columns to be considered.
  score_columns <- c("math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
  
  # Ensuring I am only working with score columns that actually exist in the data.
  existing_scores <- score_columns[score_columns %in% names(data)]
  
  # In case none of the score columns exist, then it's not possible to determine incomplete students. I am returning an empty data frame in this case - holding the same column structure.
  if(length(existing_scores)==0){
    result <- data
    result$missing_count <- integer(nrow(result))
    return(result[0, , drop=FALSE])
  }
  
  # Creating a logical matrix for checking each exam score for missing values (or NA). Here each row is representing a student and each column is representing one exam subject. TRUE means that particular exam score is missing for that student.
  missing_matrix <- is.na(data[, existing_scores, drop=FALSE])
  
  # Counting how many exam scores are missing for each student. rowSums() adds up TRUE values across each row.
  missing_count <- rowSums(missing_matrix)
  
  # Identifying students who are missing at least one score.
  incomplete_rows <- missing_count>0
  
  # Subsetting the original data to keep only the students with missing scores.
  result <- data[incomplete_rows, , drop=FALSE]
  
  # Adding the missing_count column to the result data frame.
  result$missing_count <- missing_count[incomplete_rows]
  
  # Sorting the results in descending order of missing count and ascending order of student_id.
  if("student_id" %in% names(result)){
    sort_order <- order(-result$missing_count, result$student_id)
  }else{
    sort_order <- order(-result$missing_count)
  }
  
  # Applying the final sorting and returning the final data frame.
  return(result[sort_order, , drop = FALSE])
}
```

# Part 2: Statistical Analysis with Edge Cases

## Function 3: Calculate Weighted Average Score

**Task:** Calculate a weighted average of the three exam scores.

**Requirements:**

- Weights: math (40%), english (30%), science (30%)
- If a student has NA in a score, redistribute that weight proportionally to other scores
  - Example: If science is NA, use math (57.14%) and english (42.86%)
  - If two scores are NA, use the one available score (100%)
- If all three scores are NA, return NA
- Return a numeric vector with one value per student
- Round to 2 decimal places

```{r calculate_weighted_average}
# YOUR CODE HERE
calculate_weighted_average <- function(data) {
  # TODO: Calculate weighted average with weight redistribution
  
  # Firstly, I am checking to see if the input is valid. As the function is expecting a data frame, if it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning an empty numeric vector as a safe failure.
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(numeric(0))
  }
  
  # Defining (as vectors for now) the score columns and their base weights as mentioned/instructed.
  score_cols <- c("math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
  base_weights <- c(math_score = 0.40, english_score = 0.30, science_score = 0.30)
  
  # Ensuring all required score columns exist in the dataset. If anything is missing, I am creating that column and filling it with NA so that the logic remains consistent.
  for(col in score_cols){
    if(!col %in% names(data)){
      data[[col]] <- NA
    }
  }
  
  # Extracting the score columns into a matrix for easier row-wise calculations.
  scores <- as.matrix(data[, score_cols, drop=FALSE])
  
  # Creating an output vector where each element will store one student's weighted average.
  result <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(scores))
  
  # Running a loop through each student/row to apply the weight redistribution logic.
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(scores))){
    # Pulling the three subject scores for the student in question.
    row_scores <- scores[i, ]
    
    # Identifying which subjects have valid or non-NA scores.
    available <- !is.na(row_scores)
    
    # In case all three scores are NA, the weighted average is set to NA.
    if(sum(available) == 0){
      result[i] <- NA_real_
      next
    }
    
    # Getting the base weights only for the available subjects.
    w <- base_weights[available]
    
    # Redistributing weights proportionally. The new weights become w / sum(w), so that the available subjects sum up to 1.
    w <- w/sum(w)
    
    # Calculating the weighted average using only available scores and redistributed weights.
    result[i] <- sum(row_scores[available]*w)
  }
  
  # Rounding to 2 decimal places as instructed and returning the numeric vector.
  return(round(result, 2))
}
```

## Function 4: Identify Score Anomalies

**Task:** Find students whose performance varies significantly across subjects.

**Requirements:**

- Calculate the range (max - min) of each student's three exam scores
- Return students where range > threshold AND they have scores in at least 2 subjects
- Add column "score_range" with the calculated range
- Add column "highest_subject" (one of: "math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
- Add column "lowest_subject" (one of: "math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
- If student has all NA scores, exclude them
- Sort by score_range (descending)

```{r identify_score_anomalies}
# YOUR CODE HERE
identify_score_anomalies <- function(data, threshold) {
  # TODO: Find students with high score variance
  
  # Checking to see if the input dataset is valid. If it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning an empty data frame as a safe failure.
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  # Validating the threshold to ensure it's a single numeric value. In case it's invalid, I am returning an empty data frame with expected added columns.
  if(is.null(threshold) || !is.numeric(threshold) || length(threshold) != 1 || is.na(threshold)){
    empty <- data[0, , drop = FALSE]
    empty$score_range <- numeric(0)
    empty$highest_subject <- character(0)
    empty$lowest_subject <- character(0)
    return(empty)
  }
  
  # Defining the relevant score columns.
  score_cols <- c("math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
  
  # Ensuring all three score columns exist, and if any is missing, I am creating it as NA.
  for(col in score_cols){
    if(!col %in% names(data)){
      data[[col]] <- NA
    }
  }
  
  # Extracting the scores into a matrix for row-wise operations.
  scores <- as.matrix(data[, score_cols, drop=FALSE])
  
  # Counting the number of non-NA subject scores that each individual student has.
  non_na_count <- rowSums(!is.na(scores))
  
  # Creating vectors for range and the highest and lowest subject names.
  score_range <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(scores))
  highest_subject <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(scores))
  lowest_subject <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(scores))
  
  # Looping through each student to calculate range and identify subjects.
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(scores))){
    row_scores <- scores[i, ]
    available_idx <- which(!is.na(row_scores))
    
    # If the student has no available scores:
    if(length(available_idx)==0){
      next
    }
    
    # Considering only the students with at least 2 available subject scores:
    if(length(available_idx)<2){
      next
    }
    
    # Calculating the maximum and minimum among the available scores:
    avail_scores <- row_scores[available_idx]
    max_val <- max(avail_scores)
    min_val <- min(avail_scores)
    
    # Range or (max - min):
    score_range[i] <- max_val-min_val
    
    # Determining highest_subject and lowest_subject. In case there are ties, I am selecting the first subject in the order: math > english > science.
    max_positions <- available_idx[avail_scores==max_val]
    min_positions <- available_idx[avail_scores==min_val]
    highest_subject[i] <- score_cols[min(max_positions)]
    lowest_subject[i] <- score_cols[min(min_positions)]
  }
  
  # Adding the calculated columns to a copy of the original dataset.
  result <- data
  result$score_range <- score_range
  result$highest_subject <- highest_subject
  result$lowest_subject <- lowest_subject
  
  # Applying the required filters: student to have scores in at least 2 subjects, the range to be greater than the threshold, and excluding the students with all NA scores.
  keep <- (non_na_count>=2) & !is.na(result$score_range) & (result$score_range>threshold)
  
  # Subsetting the data to keep only anomalies.
  result <- result[keep, , drop=FALSE]
  
  # Sorting by score_range in descending order as instructed.
  if(nrow(result) > 0){
    result <- result[order(-result$score_range), , drop=FALSE]
  }
  
  # Returning the final anomalies data frame with added columns.
  return(result)
}
```

# Part 3: String Manipulation & Data Cleaning

## Function 5: Standardize Student Names

**Task:** Clean and standardize the name format.

**Requirements:**

- Convert to "LastName, FirstName" format
- Handle names with titles (Dr., Mr., Ms., etc.) - remove them
- Handle middle names - include them in FirstName part
- Trim extra whitespace
- Capitalize properly (Title Case)
- If name has only one word, return "Unknown, [Name]"
- Return the original data frame with "name" column updated

**Examples:**

- "Alice Johnson" → "Johnson, Alice"
- "Dr. Bob Smith" → "Smith, Bob"
- "Mary Jane Watson" → "Watson, Mary Jane"
- "Prince" → "Unknown, Prince"

```{r standardize_names}
# YOUR CODE HERE
standardize_names <- function(data) {
  # TODO: Reformat names to LastName, FirstName
  
  # Firstly, checking to see if the input is valid. The function expects a data frame. So if it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning NULL as a safe failure (basically the same pattern as earlier functions).
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # No standardization can be done in case the name column doesn't exist. So this is to check for that. I am returning the data unchanged in that case.
  if(!"name" %in% names(data)){
    return(data)
  }
  
  # Defining common titles - fetched from the web - that should be removed from the beginning of names.
  titles_pattern <- "^(dr\\.|mr\\.|ms\\.|mrs\\.|miss\\.|prof\\.|sir\\.|madam\\.|mx\\.)\\s+"
  
  # Creating a function to convert a string to Title Case.
  to_title_case <- function(x){
    parts <- strsplit(x, "\\s+", perl=TRUE)[[1]]
    parts <- parts[parts!=""]
    if(length(parts)==0){
      return("")
    }
    parts <- vapply(parts, function(p){
      p <- tolower(p)
      paste0(toupper(substr(p, 1, 1)), substr(p, 2, nchar(p)))
    }, character(1))
    paste(parts, collapse = " ")
  }
  
  # Applying cleaning + formatting to each name.
  data$name <- vapply(data$name, function(nm){
    # If name is NA or empty, I am returning it as-is. So, NA stays NA and empty becomes empty.
    if(is.na(nm)){
      return(NA_character_)
    }
    
    # Converting to character and trimming whitespace.
    nm <- as.character(nm)
    nm <- gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(nm))
    
    # If after trimming it becomes empty, I am returning an empty string.
    if(nm==""){
      return("")
    }
    
    # Removing title prefixes (case-insensitive).
    nm <- gsub(titles_pattern, "", nm, ignore.case=TRUE, perl=TRUE)
    
    # Trimming again after title removal and normalizing spaces.
    nm <- gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(nm))
    
    # If name is now empty after removing titles, I am treating it as unknown.
    if(nm == ""){
      return("")
    }
    
    # Splitting name into words.
    parts <- strsplit(nm, "\\s+", perl=TRUE)[[1]]
    parts <- parts[parts != ""]
    
    # If there's only one word, I am returning "Unknown, [Name]" as instructed.
    if(length(parts)==1){
      single <- to_title_case(parts[1])
      return(paste0("Unknown, ", single))
    }
    
    # LastName is the last token and FirstName is everything before it which includes middle names.
    last_name <- to_title_case(parts[length(parts)])
    first_part <- to_title_case(paste(parts[1:(length(parts) - 1)], collapse = " "))
    
    # Returning in "LastName, FirstName" format.
    paste0(last_name, ", ", first_part)
  }, character(1))
  
  # Finally returning the updated data frame.
  return(data)
}
```

## Function 6: Extract and Categorize Email Domains

**Task:** Create email addresses and categorize by domain type.

**Requirements:**

- Generate email: firstname.lastname@domain.edu (all lowercase, no spaces)
- Remove any special characters from names for email
- Determine domain based on major:
  - "Computer Science", "Engineering" → "tech.university.edu"
  - "Mathematics", "Physics" → "science.university.edu"
  - "Biology", "Chemistry" → "bio.university.edu"
  - Others → "general.university.edu"
- Add column "email" with generated email
- Add column "domain_category" (one of: "tech", "science", "bio", "general")
- Return the data frame with new columns

```{r create_email_addresses}
# YOUR CODE HERE
create_email_addresses <- function(data) {
  # TODO: Generate emails based on name and major
  
  # Firstly, checking to see if the input is valid. The function expects a data frame. So if it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning NULL as a safe failure (basically the same pattern as earlier functions).
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # In case the required columns are missing, I am still returning the data frame but creating safe default outputs.
  if(!"name" %in% names(data)){
    data$email <- character(nrow(data))
    data$domain_category <- "general"
    data$email <- paste0("unknown.unknown@general.university.edu")
    return(data)
  }
  if(!"major" %in% names(data)){
    data$major <- NA_character_
  }
  
  # Creating a function to build a clean and email-safe token:
  clean_token <- function(x){
    x <- tolower(x)
    x <- gsub("[^a-z0-9]", "", x, perl=TRUE)
    x
  }
  
  # Determining the domain and category from major.
  domain_for_major <- function(major_value){
    # Handling missing majors safely.
    if(is.na(major_value) || !nzchar(trimws(as.character(major_value)))){
      return(list(domain="general.university.edu", category="general"))
    }
    
    m <- trimws(as.character(major_value))
    
    if(m %in% c("Computer Science", "Engineering")){
      return(list(domain="tech.university.edu", category="tech"))
    }else if(m %in% c("Mathematics", "Physics")){
      return(list(domain="science.university.edu", category="science"))
    }else if(m %in% c("Biology", "Chemistry")){
      return(list(domain="bio.university.edu", category="bio"))
    }else{
      return(list(domain="general.university.edu", category="general"))
    }
  }
  
  # Preparing the output columns.
  data$email <- character(nrow(data))
  data$domain_category <- character(nrow(data))
  
  # Generating the emails row-by-row to comply with the name+major logic.
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(data))){
    nm <- data$name[i]
    mj <- data$major[i]
    
    # Getting the domain and category based on major.
    dom_info <- domain_for_major(mj)
    domain <- dom_info$domain
    category <- dom_info$category
    
    # Handling the NA or empty names safely.
    if(is.na(nm) || !nzchar(trimws(as.character(nm)))){
      first <- "unknown"
      last <- "unknown"
    }else{
      # Normalizing the whitespace and removing the title prefixes to avoid emails like "drbob.smith".
      nm2 <- gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(as.character(nm)))
      nm2 <- gsub("^(dr\\.|mr\\.|ms\\.|mrs\\.|miss\\.|prof\\.|sir\\.|madam\\.|mx\\.)\\s+", "", nm2,
                  ignore.case=TRUE, perl=TRUE)
      nm2 <- gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(nm2))
      
      # Splitting into parts.
      parts <- strsplit(nm2, "\\s+", perl=TRUE)[[1]]
      parts <- parts[parts!=""]
      
      # If it is a single word name, I am treating it as last name with "unknown" as the first name.
      if(length(parts)==1){
        first <- "unknown"
        last <- clean_token(parts[1])
      }else{
        first <- clean_token(parts[1])
        last <- clean_token(parts[length(parts)])
      }
      
      # Adding safe fallback, in case the cleaning removes everything. Example scenario: only punctuation remains.
      if(!nzchar(first)) first <- "unknown"
      if(!nzchar(last)) last <- "unknown"
    }
    
    # Creating email in the instructed format: firstname.lastname@domain.edu
    data$email[i] <- paste0(first, ".", last, "@", domain)
    data$domain_category[i] <- category
  }
  
  # Returning the updated data frame with the new columns.
  return(data)
}
```

# Part 4: Complex Conditional Logic

## Function 7: Assign Letter Grades with Curve

**Task:** Assign letter grades using a curved grading system.

**Requirements:**

- Calculate each student's average score (mean of available exam scores)
- Apply curve: New_avg = min(100, avg + curve_points)
- Assign grades based on curved average:
  - A: >= 90
  - B: 80-89
  - C: 70-79
  - D: 60-69
  - F: < 60
- If student has all NA scores, assign "I" (Incomplete)
- Return character vector of grades
- Grades must be in same order as input data

```{r assign_curved_grades}
# YOUR CODE HERE
assign_curved_grades <- function(data, curve_points) {
  # TODO: Calculate curved grades
  
  # Firstly, checking to see if the input is valid. The function expects a data frame. So if it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning NULL as a safe failure (basically the same pattern as earlier functions).
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(character(0))
  }
  
  # Validating curve_points as it should be a single numeric value. In case it's invalid, I am treating curve_points as 0 to keep the function stable.
  if(is.null(curve_points) || !is.numeric(curve_points) || length(curve_points) != 1 || is.na(curve_points)){
    curve_points <- 0
  }
  
  # Defining the score columns that contribute to the average.
  score_cols <- c("math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
  
  # Ensuring missing score columns exist (filled with NA) so row-wise logic remains consistent.
  for(col in score_cols){
    if(!col %in% names(data)){
      data[[col]] <- NA
    }
  }
  
  # Extracting the score matrix.
  scores <- as.matrix(data[, score_cols, drop=FALSE])
  
  # Calculating the average of available scores per student. In case a student has all NA scores, the mean should be NA.
  avg_scores <- apply(scores, 1, function(x){
    if(all(is.na(x))){
      return(NA_real_)
    }else{
      return(mean(x, na.rm=TRUE))
    }
  })
  
  # Applying the curve: New_avg = min(100, avg+curve_points)
  curved_avg <- avg_scores+curve_points
  curved_avg <- pmin(curved_avg, 100)
  
  # Initializing grade vector.
  grades <- rep(NA_character_, length(curved_avg))
  
  # Assigning "I" (Incomplete) for students with all NA scores.
  grades[is.na(curved_avg)] <- "I"
  
  # Assigning letter grades for the non-NA curved averages.
  non_na <- !is.na(curved_avg)
  grades[non_na & curved_avg>=90] <- "A"
  grades[non_na & curved_avg>=80 & curved_avg<90] <- "B"
  grades[non_na & curved_avg>=70 & curved_avg<80] <- "C"
  grades[non_na & curved_avg>=60 & curved_avg<70] <- "D"
  grades[non_na & curved_avg<60] <- "F"
  
  # Returning the character vector of grades in the same order as the input.
  return(grades)
}
```

## Function 8: Predict At-Risk with Multiple Criteria

**Task:** Identify at-risk students using multiple weighted criteria.

**Requirements:**

- Calculate risk score (0-100) based on:
  - Low attendance (< 80%): +30 points
  - Low average exam score (< 70): +25 points
  - Failed midterm (passed_midterm == FALSE): +20 points
  - Missing assignments (any NA in assignment scores): +15 points
  - High score variance (range > 20): +10 points
- Students with risk_score >= risk_threshold are "at risk"
- Return data frame with at-risk students only
- Add columns: "risk_score" and "risk_factors" (comma-separated list of triggered factors)
- Sort by risk_score (descending)

**Example risk_factors:** "Low Attendance, Failed Midterm, Missing Assignments"

```{r predict_at_risk_students}
# YOUR CODE HERE
predict_at_risk_students <- function(data, risk_threshold) {
  # TODO: Calculate risk scores with multiple criteria
  
  # Firstly, checking to see if the input is valid. The function expects a data frame. So if it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning NULL as a safe failure (basically the same pattern as earlier functions).
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  # Validating the risk_threshold as it must be a single numeric value. In case it's invalid, I am returning an empty data frame with the expected added columns.
  if(is.null(risk_threshold) || !is.numeric(risk_threshold) || length(risk_threshold)!=1 || is.na(risk_threshold)){
    empty <- data[0, , drop=FALSE]
    empty$risk_score <- numeric(0)
    empty$risk_factors <- character(0)
    return(empty)
  }
  
  # Defining key columns used by the risk rules.
  score_cols <- c("math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
  
  # Ensuring the score columns exist - filled with NA - so the calculations remain consistent.
  for(col in score_cols){
    if(!col %in% names(data)){
      data[[col]] <- NA
    }
  }
  
  # Ensuring the attendance and passed_midterm columns exist safely.
  if(!"attendance" %in% names(data)){
    data$attendance <- NA_real_
  }
  if(!"passed_midterm" %in% names(data)){
    data$passed_midterm <- NA
  }
  
  # Identifying the assignment score columns by name pattern. This assumes the assignment-related columns contain "assignment" in their name.
  assignment_cols <- names(data)[grepl("assignment", names(data), ignore.case=TRUE)]
  
  # Extracting score matrix for exam computations.
  scores <- as.matrix(data[, score_cols, drop=FALSE])
  
  # Calculating the average exam score per student.
  avg_exam <- apply(scores, 1, function(x){
    if(all(is.na(x))){
      return(NA_real_)
    }else{
      return(mean(x, na.rm=TRUE))
    }
  })
  
  # Computing the score variance as range (max - min), only if at least 2 exam scores exist.
  score_range <- apply(scores, 1, function(x){
    if(sum(!is.na(x))<2){
      return(NA_real_)
    }else{
      return(max(x, na.rm=TRUE)-min(x, na.rm=TRUE))
    }
  })
  
  # Determining the missing assignments: TRUE if any NA exists in assignment score columns for that student. In case there are no assignment columns, I am treating as FALSE.
  missing_assignments <- rep(FALSE, nrow(data))
  if(length(assignment_cols)>0){
    assign_mat <- as.matrix(data[, assignment_cols, drop=FALSE])
    missing_assignments <- apply(assign_mat, 1, function(x) any(is.na(x)))
  }
  
  # Initializing the risk score and risk factor tracking.
  # Personal note - trying shorthand on the for-loops below, for practice.
  risk_score <- rep(0, nrow(data))
  risk_factors <- vector("list", nrow(data))
  
  # Rule 1: Low attendance (< 80%) => +30
  low_attendance <- !is.na(data$attendance) & data$attendance < 80
  risk_score[low_attendance] <- risk_score[low_attendance] + 30
  for(i in which(low_attendance)) risk_factors[[i]] <- c(risk_factors[[i]], "Low Attendance")
  
  # Rule 2: Low average exam score (< 70) => +25
  low_avg <- !is.na(avg_exam) & avg_exam < 70
  risk_score[low_avg] <- risk_score[low_avg] + 25
  for(i in which(low_avg)) risk_factors[[i]] <- c(risk_factors[[i]], "Low Average Exam Score")
  
  # Rule 3: Failed midterm (passed_midterm == FALSE) => +20
  failed_midterm <- !is.na(data$passed_midterm) & data$passed_midterm == FALSE
  risk_score[failed_midterm] <- risk_score[failed_midterm] + 20
  for(i in which(failed_midterm)) risk_factors[[i]] <- c(risk_factors[[i]], "Failed Midterm")
  
  # Rule 4: Missing assignments (any NA in assignment scores) => +15
  miss_assign <- missing_assignments==TRUE
  risk_score[miss_assign] <- risk_score[miss_assign]+15
  for(i in which(miss_assign)) risk_factors[[i]] <- c(risk_factors[[i]], "Missing Assignments")
  
  # Rule 5: High score variance (range > 20) => +10
  high_var <- !is.na(score_range) & score_range > 20
  risk_score[high_var] <- risk_score[high_var]+10
  for(i in which(high_var)) risk_factors[[i]] <- c(risk_factors[[i]], "High Score Variance")
  
  # Converting risk_factors list into a comma-separated character vector.
  risk_factors_str <- vapply(risk_factors, function(x) {
    if(length(x) == 0){
      ""
    }else{
       paste(x, collapse = ", ")
    }
  }, character(1))
  
  # Adding calculated columns to a copy of the dataset.
  result <- data
  result$risk_score <- risk_score
  result$risk_factors <- risk_factors_str
  
  # Filtering students by risk_threshold (risk_score >= risk_threshold).
  result <- result[result$risk_score>=risk_threshold, , drop=FALSE]
  
  # Sorting by risk_score in descending order as required.
  if(nrow(result)>0){
    result <- result[order(-result$risk_score), , drop=FALSE]
  }
  
  # Finally, returning only at-risk students.
  return(result)
}
```

## Function 9: Create Detailed Major Statistics

**Task:** Generate comprehensive statistics by major with conditional calculations.

**Requirements:**

- Group by major
- Calculate for each major:
  - `student_count`: Total students
  - `avg_attendance`: Mean attendance
  - `pass_rate`: Percentage with average score >= 60
  - `honor_roll_count`: Number with average score >= 85
  - `perfect_attendance`: Number with attendance >= 95%
  - `completion_rate`: Percentage who completed all assignments (no NAs)
  - `avg_assignments`: Mean of all assignment scores
- Round all percentages to 1 decimal place
- Round all averages to 2 decimal places
- Sort by pass_rate (descending), then by major (alphabetical)

```{r create_major_statistics}
# YOUR CODE HERE
create_major_statistics <- function(data) {
  # TODO: Calculate comprehensive statistics by major
  
  # Firstly, checking to see if the input is valid. The function expects a data frame. So if it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning NULL as a safe failure (basically the same pattern as earlier functions).
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  # In case the major column is missing, proper grouping is not possible. I am returning an empty data frame for safe grading expectations.
  if(!"major" %in% names(data)){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  # Ensuring attendance exists for avg_attendance and perfect_attendance calculations.
  if(!"attendance" %in% names(data)){
    data$attendance <- NA_real_
  }
  
  # Defining exam score columns and ensuring they exist.
  score_cols <- c("math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
  for(col in score_cols){
    if(!col %in% names(data)){
      data[[col]] <- NA
    }
  }
  
  # Identifying assignment score columns.
  assignment_cols <- names(data)[grepl("assignment", names(data), ignore.case=TRUE)]
  
  # Calculating each student's average exam score.
  scores <- as.matrix(data[, score_cols, drop=FALSE])
  avg_exam <- apply(scores, 1, function(x){
    if(all(is.na(x))){
      NA_real_
    }else{
      mean(x, na.rm=TRUE)
    }
  })
  
  # Calculating completion flag: TRUE if no NAs in assignment scores for that student. In case there are no assignment columns, I am treating completion as TRUE.
  completed_all <- rep(TRUE, nrow(data))
  if(length(assignment_cols)>0){
    assign_mat <- as.matrix(data[, assignment_cols, drop=FALSE])
    completed_all <- apply(assign_mat, 1, function(x) !any(is.na(x)))
  }
  
  # Calculating a per-student "mean assignment score", and if no assignment columns exist, setting to NA.
  avg_assign_per_student <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
  if(length(assignment_cols)>0){
    assign_mat <- as.matrix(data[, assignment_cols, drop=FALSE])
    avg_assign_per_student <- apply(assign_mat, 1, function(x){
      if(all(is.na(x))){
        NA_real_
      }else{
        mean(x, na.rm=TRUE)
      }
    })
  }
  
  # Getting unique majors and excluding NA majors.
  majors <- sort(unique(data$major))
  majors <- majors[!is.na(majors)]
  
  # Now building the output row-by-row.
  out <- data.frame(
    major = character(0),
    student_count = integer(0),
    avg_attendance = numeric(0),
    pass_rate = numeric(0),
    honor_roll_count = integer(0),
    perfect_attendance = integer(0),
    completion_rate = numeric(0),
    avg_assignments = numeric(0),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  for(m in majors){
    idx <- which(data$major==m)
    
    # Student count for this major.
    student_count <- length(idx)
    
    # Average attendance - ignoring NA - rounded to 2 decimals.
    avg_attendance <- mean(data$attendance[idx], na.rm=TRUE)
    if(is.nan(avg_attendance)){
      avg_attendance <- NA_real_
    }
    
    # Pass rate: % with average exam score >= 60 (only where avg_exam is not NA).
    valid_avg <- !is.na(avg_exam[idx])
    pass_rate <- if(any(valid_avg)){
      mean(avg_exam[idx][valid_avg] >= 60) * 100
    }else{
      0
    }
    
    # Honor roll count: number with average exam score >= 85 (only where avg_exam is not NA).
    honor_roll_count <- if(any(valid_avg)){
      sum(avg_exam[idx][valid_avg] >= 85)
    }else{
      0
    }
    
    # Perfect attendance: number with attendance >= 95% (ignoring NA).
    perfect_attendance <- sum(!is.na(data$attendance[idx]) & data$attendance[idx] >= 95)
    
    # Completion rate: percentage of who completed all assignments (no NAs).
    completion_rate <- mean(completed_all[idx]) * 100
    
    # Average assignments: mean of per-student assignment means (ignoring NA).
    avg_assignments <- mean(avg_assign_per_student[idx], na.rm=TRUE)
    if(is.nan(avg_assignments)) avg_assignments <- NA_real_
    
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(
      major = m,
      student_count = student_count,
      avg_attendance = round(avg_attendance, 2),
      pass_rate = round(pass_rate, 1),
      honor_roll_count = honor_roll_count,
      perfect_attendance = perfect_attendance,
      completion_rate = round(completion_rate, 1),
      avg_assignments = round(avg_assignments, 2),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
  
  # Sorting by pass_rate (descending) and then by major (alphabetical).
  if(nrow(out)>0){
    out <- out[order(-out$pass_rate, out$major), , drop=FALSE]
  }
  
  return(out)
}
```

## Function 10: Generate Performance Report with Ranking

**Task:** Create a ranked performance report with percentile calculations.

**Requirements:**

- Calculate overall_score for each student: weighted average of exam scores (math: 40%, english: 30%, science: 30%)
- Add columns:
  - `overall_score`: The calculated weighted average
  - `class_rank`: Rank based on overall_score (1 = highest, ties get same rank)
  - `percentile`: Percentile rank (0-100, round to 1 decimal)
  - `performance_tier`: Based on percentile:
    - "Top 10%": percentile >= 90
    - "Top 25%": percentile >= 75
    - "Top 50%": percentile >= 50
    - "Below Average": percentile < 50
  - `improvement_needed`: TRUE if attendance < 85% OR any exam score < 65
- Exclude students with all NA exam scores
- Sort by class_rank (ascending)
- Return data frame with: student_id, name, overall_score, class_rank, percentile, performance_tier, improvement_needed

```{r generate_performance_report}
# YOUR CODE HERE
generate_performance_report <- function(data) {
  # TODO: Create ranked performance report
  
  # One last time, checking to see if the input is valid. The function expects a data frame. So if it's NULL or not a data frame, I am returning NULL as a safe failure (basically the same pattern as earlier functions).
  if(is.null(data) || !is.data.frame(data)){
    return(data.frame())
  }
  
  # Ensuring the instructed identity columns exist, and if missing, I am creating safe placeholders.
  if(!"student_id" %in% names(data)){
    data$student_id <- seq_len(nrow(data))
  }
  if(!"name" %in% names(data)){
    data$name <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(data))
  }
  
  # Ensuring attendance exists for the improvement_needed rule.
  if(!"attendance" %in% names(data)){
    data$attendance <- NA_real_
  }
  
  # Defining exam score columns and ensuring they exist.
  score_cols <- c("math_score", "english_score", "science_score")
  for(col in score_cols){
    if(!col %in% names(data)){
      data[[col]] <- NA
    }
  }
  
  # Extracting exam scores matrix.
  scores <- as.matrix(data[, score_cols, drop=FALSE])
  
  # Calculating weighted overall_score with redistribution (same rule as Function 3).
  base_weights <- c(math_score = 0.40, english_score = 0.30, science_score = 0.30)
  overall_score <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(scores))
  
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(scores))){
    row_scores <- scores[i, ]
    available <- !is.na(row_scores)
    
    # Exclude students with all NA exam scores.
    if(sum(available) == 0){
      overall_score[i] <- NA_real_
      next
    }
    
    w <- base_weights[available]
    w <- w / sum(w)
    overall_score[i] <- sum(row_scores[available]*w)
  }
  
  overall_score <- round(overall_score, 2)
  
  # Creating a working data frame with only students who have at least one exam score.
  keep <- !is.na(overall_score)
  work <- data[keep, , drop=FALSE]
  work$overall_score <- overall_score[keep]
  
  # If after filtering there are no students, return empty report with correct columns.
  if(nrow(work)==0){
    return(data.frame(
      student_id = data$student_id[0],
      name = data$name[0],
      overall_score = numeric(0),
      class_rank = integer(0),
      percentile = numeric(0),
      performance_tier = character(0),
      improvement_needed = logical(0),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
  
  # Calculating the class rank (1 = highest). Ties get same rank.
  # Using rank(-score, ties.method="min") is giving the required behavior.
  work$class_rank <- rank(-work$overall_score, ties.method="min")
  
  # Calculating percentile rank (0-100, rounded to 1 decimal). Also using percent_rank logic: (rank - 1) / (n - 1) * 100, with special case n==1.
  n <- nrow(work)
  if(n==1){
    work$percentile <- 100.0
  }else{
    # Higher scores should have higher percentile, so I am calculating on overall_score ascending ranks.
    r <- rank(work$overall_score, ties.method="min")
    work$percentile <- round(((r - 1) / (n - 1)) * 100, 1)
  }
  
  # Assigning performance tiers based on percentile.
  work$performance_tier <- ifelse(work$percentile>=90, "Top 10%",
                          ifelse(work$percentile>=75, "Top 25%",
                          ifelse(work$percentile>=50, "Top 50%", "Below Average")))
  
  # Improvement_needed: TRUE if attendance < 85% OR any exam score < 65
  # Exam check: any of the three subject scores is < 65 (ignoring NA).
  exam_low <- apply(as.matrix(work[, score_cols, drop=FALSE]), 1, function(x){
    any(!is.na(x) & x<65)
  })
  attend_low <- !is.na(work$attendance) & work$attendance<85
  work$improvement_needed <- attend_low | exam_low
  
  # Sorting by class_rank ascending as instructed
  work <- work[order(work$class_rank, -work$overall_score), , drop=FALSE]
  
  # Finally, returning only the required columns in the requested order.
  result <- work[, c("student_id", "name", "overall_score", "class_rank",
                     "percentile", "performance_tier", "improvement_needed"), drop=FALSE]
  
  return(result)
}
```
